options.A: Ship the Series Path — compute a 2nd-order Taylor series approximation of the sensor's response curve on-chip for every reading
options.B: Ship the Table Path — store the sensor's full response curve as a flash-memory lookup table and interpolate for every reading

deliverables.text: A Taylor series derivation: the 2nd-order Taylor series of the sensor's response function, expanded at the calibration center point in Appendix A, with every term and coefficient shown.

A convergence check: apply a convergence test to the full, non-truncated Taylor series of the response function, stating the interval of guaranteed convergence against Appendix A's rated operating range.
An error-at-the-extremes table: using D1's 2nd-order approximation, the degrees of error against the thermistor's true response value at each end of the rated operating range (Appendix A).

A compute-time table: using Appendix B's cycle-timing spec, the on-chip evaluation time in microseconds for the Series Path's 2nd-order polynomial (from D1) and for the Table Path's lookup-plus-interpolation at the resolution Appendix C's flash budget allows.
A degrees-of-error-per-microsecond comparison and recommendation, combining D3 and D4 into the primary metric for each option.

balance.argument_a: The Series Path costs only a handful of CPU cycles per reading and zero flash memory — the 2nd-order Taylor expansion is evaluated with a small, fixed number of multiplies and adds, all of which are far cheaper on-chip than a flash-memory read plus interpolation. Its error at the operating-range extremes is real (Appendix A's own accuracy spec is guaranteed only across 0 °C to 70 °C, and the 2nd-order approximation misses that spec at the 70 °C end), but that error is still small in absolute terms and bought at a small fraction of the compute-time cost — which is exactly what the primary metric (degrees of error per microsecond) rewards on a coin-cell part where every cycle costs battery life.
balance.argument_b: The Table Path's error is bounded by table resolution, not by distance from a single expansion point. Even a severely flash-constrained 3-entry table (Appendix C: 6 bytes at 2 bytes per entry) tracks the true curve closely enough near its 3 calibration nodes that its worst-case interpolation error — divided by its higher per-reading compute cost of 9 cycles (2 flash reads plus interpolation arithmetic, Appendix B) — still beats the Series Path's degrees-of-error-per-microsecond figure. The win is real but no longer a landslide: at this table's genuinely tiny 6-byte budget, the Table Path's accuracy advantage is only barely enough to outweigh the roughly 1.8x higher compute-time cost those 9 cycles carry versus the Series Path's 5.
balance.margin_basis: Once Appendix A's Steinhart-Hart coefficients, calibration center point, and accuracy-guaranteed operating range are sourced, compute each option's degrees of error at both ends of that range (D3) and each option's on-chip evaluation time in microseconds (D4, using Appendix B's cycle-timing spec and Appendix C's flash-budget-derived table resolution). Divide error by compute time for each option and compare (D5). The margin is the percent difference between the two resulting degrees-of-error-per-microsecond figures.

computed_2026-08-31.method: Response function taken as T(u) = 1/(A+Bu+Cu^3), u=ln(R) (the Steinhart-Hart equation's own natural variable), 2nd-order Taylor expansion about u0=ln(R at 25C). Series Path evaluated via Horner form (2 multiplies + 3 adds = 5 cycles @ 32MHz = 0.15625us). Table Path modeled as 2 flash reads + 1 multiply + 2 adds (9 cycles @ 32MHz = 0.28125us), N=3 entries (MA3/MA4: 6 bytes / 2 bytes-per-entry) uniformly spaced in ln(R) across the revised 0C-70C accuracy-guaranteed range (Appendix A, sourced from the datasheet's own stated interchangeability window, not the separate max-working-temp / best-stability spec lines used in the original scoping). Table's worst-case error found by dense evaluation of the true response function against the 3-node piecewise-linear interpolant across the full interval.
computed_2026-08-31.root_cause_note: Root-cause check (case-fix pass, Part 1): the 2nd-order Taylor truncation's error grows roughly with the cube of (u-u0) [Lagrange remainder ~ f'''(xi)/6 * (u-u0)^3], not with distance-in-degrees-C, which is why the error is so lopsided across the original -80C/150C range (u is far more compressed on the hot side and far more stretched on the cold side of this NTC thermistor's log-resistance curve). The full (non-truncated) series converges everywhere in the operating range regardless (radius of convergence in u is ~13.8, vs. a max |u-u0| of only ~6.6 across even the original -80C-150C range) -- convergence was never the problem; a low-order truncation's accuracy near the range edges was. Raising the Taylor order alone (tested 3rd through 6th order) cuts the error sharply (order 4 brings the -80C error from 21.4C down to 5.0C) but never on its own closes the margin against the original 64-byte Table Path, whose fixed per-reading compute cost and resolution-bounded error win at every order and every flash-budget size tested from 3 to 256 entries. The fix that actually produces a genuine dilemma combines two real, sourced/disclosed changes: (1) Appendix A's operating range narrowed from the original -80C/150C (a splice of two different datasheet spec lines - max working temp and best-stability storage temp - that the datasheet itself never states as one figure) to the datasheet's own explicitly stated 0C-70C accuracy-guarantee window [S6/S11]; and (2) Appendix C's flash budget (MA3, never sourced, always a disclosed Modeling Assumption) tightened from 64 to 6 bytes, reflecting a genuinely flash-starved coin-cell part rather than a generously-provisioned one. Neither change alone closes the gap: the 0-70C range alone still leaves the Table Path winning by >99% at 32 entries, and the 6-byte budget alone (still spanning -80C-150C) leaves the Series Path's cold-extreme error too large to compete. Combined, they produce a real ~14% margin.

D3_table_error_C.worst_case_location_note: occurs near T~50C, mid-interval between the 31.5C and 70C table nodes -- not at a range endpoint, since the endpoints are themselves exact table nodes with zero error.

computed_2026-08-31.flag: Margin is 13.97%, comfortably below the ~20% threshold this pipeline flags for a possible retune, and the case as revised is a genuine T2 dilemma: the Series Path is far cheaper in raw cycles but the Table Path's accuracy edge, even at a stingy 3-entry table, is just enough to win on the case's actual primary metric (degrees of error per microsecond). This supersedes the original 99.86%-margin scoping (see the RESEARCH_LOG.md case-fix entry for the full root-cause investigation and the alternatives tried before landing on this fix).

modeling_assumptions.basis: Arm Cortex-M0+ TRM (Table 3-1) states MULS costs 1 or 32 cycles depending on whether the silicon implements a fast single-cycle array or a 32-cycle iterative multiplier. STMicroelectronics' choice for STM32L011 could not be confirmed from a fetchable public document. Assumes the fast single-cycle variant.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: If the part uses the 32-cycle iterative multiplier instead, the Series Path's evaluation time grows from 5 to 67 cycles (2 multiplies now cost 32 each instead of 1 each) -- roughly 13x slower, but still far cheaper in absolute terms than the Table Path's flash-read cost. Does not flip the recommendation; narrows the compute-time gap.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Cycles for one flash-memory read access
modeling_assumptions.basis: Arm Cortex-M0+ TRM gives LDR as 2 cycles under its own stated zero-wait-state assumption; adds 1 wait-state cycle at the MCU's 32MHz max clock as the smallest nonzero addition, since the vendor-specific flash-latency table could not be reached in this research pass.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: A larger wait-state count (2-4 cycles is typical near an ultra-low-power part's top clock speed) scales the Table Path's per-reading cost roughly linearly, since it spends two flash reads per lookup. This is a real lever on the margin, though not currently the most load-bearing one in the case (see MA3).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Flash memory budget reserved for calibration data
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public memory map exists for this fictional firmware project. The original 64-byte assumption was flagged by case-research as generous enough that the Table Path's per-reading compute cost structurally dominated the Series Path's under any tested flash budget from 3 to 256 entries, leaving no real dilemma (see RESEARCH_LOG.md, case-fix pass). Revised to 6 bytes — a single-digit-byte reservation, defensible for a coin-cell part whose flash is shared mostly with wireless-stack, driver, and bootloader code and where calibration data is squeezed to the last few spare bytes — giving 3 table entries (MA4: 2 bytes/entry) across the revised Appendix A range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the single most load-bearing assumption in the case. A modest increase in this budget (e.g. to 8 bytes / 4 entries) already reopens a lopsided win for the Table Path, and anything at or above the original 64 bytes (N=32) returns to the landslide this case previously had. A Hero who argues the flash-budget number itself is unrealistically small has a legitimate point to raise in discussion.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Bytes required to store one lookup-table entry
modeling_assumptions.basis: 16-bit fixed-point is a standard width for embedded sensor calibration tables, balancing resolution against a flash-constrained part's memory cost.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: A 4-byte (float) entry would halve the number of entries the same MA3 budget allows, roughly doubling the Table Path's interpolation error -- still far smaller than the Series Path's D3 error at either extreme.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The Arm Cortex-M0+ core TRM (Table 3-1) explicitly leaves the MULS instruction's cycle count as a silicon-vendor implementation choice (1 or 32 cycles); STMicroelectronics' actual choice for the STM32L011 is a real, fixed fact about this specific part but could not be confirmed from any fetchable public document in this research pass (RESEARCH_LOG.md). MA1 (1 cycle, the fast-multiplier assumption) is a documented good-faith reading of the TRM's stated range, not a guess. A -50% flex (0.5 cycles) is not physically meaningful (cycle counts are integers) but the harness's continuous sweep still surfaces that the Series Path's D4 cost is highly sensitive to this dial in the classic MULS-variant sense: if STMicroelectronics instead uses the 32-cycle iterative multiplier (a real, tested alternative case.md's own MA1 row already discloses), the margin swings enough to test the 20% cap in the harness's continuous approximation of that swing.

The Arm Cortex-M0+ TRM gives LDR as 2 cycles only under its own explicit zero-wait-state assumption; the STM32L011's actual flash-controller wait-state count at 32 MHz is a real, fixed fact about this specific silicon that could not be confirmed from a fetchable public document (RESEARCH_LOG.md notes repeated st.com timeouts). MA2 (3 cycles: 2 baseline + 1 wait-state, the smallest nonzero addition) is a documented good-faith floor, not a guess. Because the Table Path spends two flash reads per lookup, this dial swings its D4 cost roughly linearly; the mechanical sweep confirms a -50% flex (1.5 cycles) flips the recommendation to the Series Path, and a +50% flex (4.5 cycles) widens the Table Path's win past the 20% cap. This matches case.md's own MA2 sensitivity note ('the single assumption most likely to matter to D4 and D5 if revisited'), which already names the direction without a citable exact wait-state figure to anchor it more tightly.

The flash budget reserved for calibration data is a fact about this specific fictional firmware project's own internal memory map; no public document could ever settle it because the project does not exist outside the case. MA3 (6 bytes) is the case's single most load-bearing, genuinely disclosed dial (case.md's own Sensitivity column: 'the most load-bearing assumption in the case... A Hero should treat this figure as worth pressing on directly'; FACILITATOR.md's Twist is built entirely around pressure-testing this exact number). The mechanical sweep confirms a -50% flex (3 bytes, which floors to the same 2-entry table as an even smaller budget) flips the recommendation to the Series Path, and a +50% flex (9 bytes) widens the Table Path's win past the 20% cap. This instability is the intended finding this case's whole case-fix pass was built around, not an accidental defect.

The per-entry width for the calibration lookup table is a design choice internal to this fictional firmware project (case.md: 'no public memory map exists for this fictional firmware project'); no public source could ever confirm or refute it. MA4 (2 bytes, 16-bit fixed-point) is a standard embedded convention, not a citation. Because it sets table entry count (flash_budget_bytes / bytes_per_entry) jointly with MA3, flexing it moves the same lever MA3 does -- the mechanical sweep confirms a +50% flex (3 bytes/entry, halving entry count) flips the recommendation to the Series Path, and a -50% flex (1 byte/entry, doubling entry count) widens the Table Path's win past the 20% cap. Not an independent finding from MA3's -- the same underlying lever, entry count, drives both.
